profiles.label: AI workstation
profiles.rationale: Running language models locally is bounded by VRAM before anything else: a model that does not fit in memory does not run slowly, it does not run. 12 GB is the floor for a comfortable 7B–14B at reasonable quantisation. The used market prices cards on frame rates, so memory capacity is the thing most reliably underpriced — which is what makes kr per GB the metric worth sorting on.

requirements.label: Nvidia GPU
requirements.why: The local-model toolchain is CUDA-bound in practice. ROCm support on consumer Radeons is partial and worse on Windows, so a Radeon is not a cheaper way to buy the same capability.

requirements.label: 12 GB VRAM
requirements.why: Below this, useful models will not fit in memory.

requirements.label: 32 GB system RAM
requirements.why: Datasets, notebooks and a VM or two will thrash 16 GB.

profiles.label: Gaming
profiles.rationale: No bespoke metric here, on purpose. Gaming is what the used market prices for, so the market is already the benchmark and the best buy is simply the largest discount to the index that still clears a playable memory floor. Inventing a performance score would mean shipping a benchmark table nobody validated, to rank listings the price data already ranks correctly.

requirements.label: 8 GB VRAM
requirements.why: Below 8 GB, current titles force texture settings down.

requirements.label: 16 GB system RAM
requirements.why: The practical minimum for modern titles.

profiles.label: Home server / NAS
profiles.rationale: A machine that runs continuously is judged on the bill it generates and the storage it holds, not on peak throughput. A 300 W gaming card idling in a cupboard is a liability rather than a feature, so a TDP ceiling is a genuine requirement and not a preference.

requirements.label: 1 TB storage
requirements.why: Anything less is not worth dedicating a machine to.

requirements.label: GPU under 100 W
requirements.why: A high-TDP card runs up the electricity bill 24/7.
